dedupe_keys.name: titchwell marsh coastal change project managed realignment north norfolk

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes the Titchwell Marsh Coastal Change Project at the RSPB reserve on the North Norfolk coast, England, part of a Special Protection Area and Special Area of Conservation, where local sea level may rise 68 cm to more than 80 cm by 2100 and seawalls protecting freshwater habitats faced erosion. The western wall was strengthened and a new wall, the Parrinder wall, built, while a breach in September 2011 let the tide into the brackish marsh, which is turning into saltmarsh and mudflat that also buffer the new wall. Freshwater habitats are now behind 5.8 m AOD defences with a 1 in 30 year standard, expected to hold for 50 years. Lost avocet nesting habitat was offset by new islands at Titchwell and new habitat at the RSPB's Frampton Marsh and Freiston Shore reserves. Planning consent came in July 2009; the budget was about 2.01 million euros, half from EU LIFE+, with WREN, SITA Trust and the Crown Estate. The page, published in 2015 and updated in 2026, is accessible online as free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal with links to the RSPB project pages. Caveats: work was limited to a three-month window each year, which stretched delivery to three years and hit visitor numbers. It illustrates nature-based coastal flood and sea level rise hazard reduction and climate adaptation; related records are the Hesketh Out Marsh and Hedwige and Prosper polders case studies.
name: Titchwell Marsh coastal change project, managed realignment (North Norfolk)
organisations: Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB)
outcomes: Managed realignment converted brackish marsh to saltmarsh and, with strengthened and new walls at 5.8 m AOD, protects the reserve's freshwater habitats for about 50 years.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study from the LIFE programme and the RSPB
